title: Extreme Close-Up (ECU)
description: An extreme close-up, or extreme close up shot, fills the frame with one small feature: an eye, a mouth, a fingertip, a trigger. Surrounding space disappears; the crop is tighter than a whole face.

sections.title: Narrative function

blocks.text: Size is a sentence. An extreme close-up says the scene is this fragment: a pupil tightening, a lip splitting, a safety clicking off.

Cutting between such fragments can turn looking into a physical confrontation, as in a standoff built from eyes instead of bodies. It is the wrong tool when the actor still needs a whole face to play the line.
If you can still see hairline and chin together, you have not arrived at this size. Use it when a detail is the event, then get out before the texture becomes a poster.

sections.title: How it works

blocks.text: Pick the anatomical landmark that hits the frame lines. Camera distance and focal length are separate from the crop: a 75mm or 100mm a few feet back keeps facial proportion; a wide lens inches from the skin balloons the nose.
A macro is only required when the feature is truly small, such as an iris or a watch gear. Tight framing, macro optics, and shallow depth of field are three different choices.
Light a small source if you want pore and scar; wrap if you want the fragment to stay readable. Prompt the exact feature and the crop (brow to upper cheek, mouth only), not a vague tight close-up.

sections.title: When to use it

blocks.text: Use it when a detail is the scene: the eye that decides to fire, the mouth that will not speak. Do not use it as a default portrait or for ordinary dialogue; the rest of the person is information you have thrown away.

sections.title: Compared with similar shots

blocks.text: A Choker Shot still holds a whole face from hairline to chin. A Close-Up keeps head and upper shoulders.
An extreme close-up is a fragment, not a portrait. An Insert Shot can be this tight, but an insert is a story object or hand fact, not a size.
If the frame still includes both eyes and a mouth as a face, you are not here yet.

sections.title: In film

blocks.text: In The Good, the Bad and the Ugly, eyes and faces dominate the final standoff montage until looking becomes the gunfight. The Passion of Joan of Arc puts interrogation pressure on facial fragments.
Persona uses faces so close that identity starts to fuse. Borrow the grammar of fragment versus whole, not a poster of an iris.

sections.title: Prompt it

blocks.text: Lead with the crop, then the feature. Example: Extreme close-up of [Subject], a single feature filling the frame, pores and texture, tighter than forehead-to-chin.
Name which feature (left eye, mouth, fingertip, trigger) and what must stay sharp. Do not write tight close-up, choker, or macro unless you actually need those.
For video, lock the camera, keep the feature in frame, and allow only a blink, a swallow, or a tiny gaze shift.

Extreme close-up of an older watchmaker’s eyes as she decides whether to open a sealed mechanism. Frame from brow to upper cheek, natural skin texture, tiny shift in gaze and controlled breathing. Restrained light, stable focus, no cosmetic smoothing or wide-angle facial distortion.

sections.title: What usually goes wrong

blocks.text: The usual wrong cousin is a Choker Shot or a Close-Up: the whole face still reads. The tell is hairline and chin both present, or shoulders sneaking in.
The other tell is wide-angle distortion from parking a short lens on the nose. Fix: name the feature, crop inside the face, and pick a longer lens or a true macro only if the object is small.

sections.title: Questions

blocks.text: What is Extreme Close-Up in film?

An extreme close-up is a shot size that fills the frame with one small feature such as an eye, a mouth, or a fingertip. It is tighter than a whole-face crop, so surrounding space becomes secondary or disappears.
Extreme Close-Up vs Choker Shot

A choker still shows a complete face from hairline to chin. An extreme close-up is a fragment: one feature, not the whole portrait. If both eyes and the mouth read as a face, you are in choker or close-up territory.
When should I use Extreme Close-Up?
Use it when the detail is the event: a trigger, an eye, a cracked lip. Skip it for ordinary talk, beauty portraits, or any beat that still needs the rest of the head and shoulders.
How do I prompt Extreme Close-Up for AI image or video?

Write Extreme close-up of [Subject], name the single feature, and say it fills the frame tighter than forehead-to-chin. Add pores and texture if you need skin fact. For video, lock off and allow only a tiny motion in that feature.
